sections.h: The son of David in the Psalms of Solomon
sections.b: Psalms of Solomon 17-18, written by devout Jews after Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC (Gray), pray for "their king, the son of David" (Psalms of Solomon 17:23). He will cleanse Jerusalem of the nations, conquer "by the word of his mouth", gather the tribes and rule the nations, trusting in God and not in horses or gold; he is "pure from sin" and made strong by God's spirit (Psalms of Solomon 17:24-42). The manuscripts call him christos kyrios, "the Lord Messiah" (Psalms of Solomon 17:36), a phrase many scholars think rendered "the LORD's anointed"; Psalm 18 speaks of "the Lord's Messiah" (Psalms of Solomon 18:8). Ryle and James saw in the portrait "the merely human nature of the Messiah". The hope stands behind the Gospels' "Son of David" and Luke 2:11, though the New Testament never quotes the book.
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 17:21-46; Psalms of Solomon 18:5-9; Luke 2:11; Luke 2:26; Matthew 1:1; Matthew 21:9

common: The Psalms of Solomon expected a human king of David's line who would free Jerusalem from Rome.
uncommon: Some scholars have suspected a Christian hand in the phrase "the Lord Messiah" (Psalms of Solomon 17:36); Ryle and James rejected the idea.

sections.h: The oath to David remembered after Pompey
sections.b: "You, Lord, chose David to be king over Israel, and you swore to him about his offspring forever that his royal line would never come to an end before you" (Psalms of Solomon 17:5). The psalm accuses the Hasmonean priest-kings of taking a throne God had not promised them (Psalms of Solomon 17:6-8) and prays that God will raise up the son of David at his chosen time (Psalms of Solomon 17:23).
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 17:5-8; Psalms of Solomon 17:23; 2 Samuel 7:12-16; Psalm 89:3-4

sections.b: Psalms of Solomon 17 begins and ends with God's kingship: "Lord, you are our King forever and ever" (Psalms of Solomon 17:1), "the kingdom of our God is over the nations forever" (Psalms of Solomon 17:4), "The Lord himself is our King forever and ever" (Psalms of Solomon 17:51). The coming son of David rules under God: "The Lord himself is his King" (Psalms of Solomon 17:38).
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 17:1-4; Psalms of Solomon 17:38; Psalms of Solomon 17:51; Mark 1:15

sections.h: Kings who were not of David's line
sections.b: Psalms of Solomon 17 charges that "sinners" seized what God had not promised them and "laid waste David's throne" (Psalms of Solomon 17:6-8). Gray identified them with the later Hasmoneans, who took the title of king from Aristobulus I (104 BC) until Pompey deposed Aristobulus II in 63 BC; the poet sees Pompey as God's punishment on them (Psalms of Solomon 17:9-11).
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 17:5-11; Psalms of Solomon 17:22

sections.h: "The devout" of the Psalms of Solomon
sections.b: The Psalms of Solomon call their own circle hosioi, "the devout", the Greek of Hebrew ḥasidim (Gray). They gather in "the assemblies of the devout", flee to the deserts when Jerusalem falls (Psalms of Solomon 17:18-20), bear God's discipline patiently and hope for the son of David. Whether they were Pharisees, as Gray and Ryle and James held, or another group, is discussed on the book's opening pages.
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 9:6; Psalms of Solomon 10:7; Psalms of Solomon 14:2; Psalms of Solomon 17:18-20

sections.h: The Psalms of Solomon and the Pharisees
sections.b: Gray called the Psalms of Solomon the work of "one or more of the Pharisees": their piety, their opposition to the non-Davidic Hasmonean kings, their hope for the Messiah, their belief in a future life, and their teaching on free will, which he found "almost exactly paralleled" in Josephus's account of the Pharisees (Jewish War 2.8.14). See Psalms of Solomon 9:7, "What we do lies in the choice and power of our own souls."
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 9:7; Psalms of Solomon 12:6; Psalms of Solomon 17:5-8

sections.h: "What we do lies in the choice and power of our own souls"
sections.b: In the Greek, Psalms of Solomon 9:7 says our deeds lie "in the choice and power of our soul", and 9:9 that whoever does right "stores up life for himself with the Lord". The same psalm rests its hope on God's choice of Abraham's offspring and his covenant (Psalms of Solomon 9:17-19), and another says God knows the heart "before anything happens" (Psalms of Solomon 14:5). Ryle and James weighed reading 9:7 as a paradox like Mishnah Avot's "Everything is foreseen; and freewill is given"; Gray rejected that reading.
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 9:7-10; Psalms of Solomon 9:17-19; Psalms of Solomon 14:5; Sirach 15:14-17; Deuteronomy 30:19

sections.h: Mercy in the Psalms of Solomon
sections.b: Nearly every psalm in the second half of the Psalms of Solomon ends on mercy: "The Lord's mercy is on Israel's house forever and ever" (Psalms of Solomon 9:20; compare 11:9; 13:11; 17:51; 18:10). The Greek eleos usually stands for Hebrew ḥesed, "loyal love". The coming age is "the day of mercy" (Psalms of Solomon 18:6).
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 9:16-20; Psalms of Solomon 13:11; Psalms of Solomon 18:1-6

sections.h: God's discipline in the Psalms of Solomon
sections.b: "Happy the man whom the Lord keeps in mind with a rebuke" (Psalms of Solomon 10:1). The book calls God's discipline the mark of a father's love: "he will correct the righteous like a son he loves" (Psalms of Solomon 13:8), "as one disciplines a firstborn, an only son" (Psalms of Solomon 18:4). The image is the father's, not a rule for raising children; compare Proverbs 3:12 and Hebrews 12:5-11.
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 10:1-3; Psalms of Solomon 13:7-9; Psalms of Solomon 18:4-5; Proverbs 3:11-12; Hebrews 12:5-11

sections.h: Exile and homecoming in the Psalms of Solomon
sections.b: Psalms of Solomon 9 confesses that Israel was scattered "among every nation, just as God had said" (Psalms of Solomon 9:2), and Psalm 11 pictures the return: Jerusalem on a height sees her children gathered from east and west (Psalms of Solomon 11:3), a passage that runs close to Baruch 5:5-8.
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 9:1-2; Psalms of Solomon 11:1-9; Baruch 5:5-8

sections.h: The tribes gathered by the son of David
sections.b: The son of David "will judge the tribes of the people made holy" and "divide them up by their tribes on the land" (Psalms of Solomon 17:28, 17:30); "Happy are those who live in those days, to see the good things of Israel in the gathering of the tribes" (Psalms of Solomon 17:50).
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 17:28-31; Psalms of Solomon 17:50; Matthew 19:28; Luke 22:30

sections.b: "For God's sign is on the righteous, to save them"; the sinners bear "the sign of destruction" on their foreheads (Psalms of Solomon 15:8, 15:10). The image stands between Ezekiel 9:4 and Revelation 7:3.
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 15:8-10; Ezekiel 9:4; Revelation 7:3; Revelation 9:4

sections.h: The devout as the trees of life
sections.b: "His devout ones are the Lord's paradise, the trees of life" (Psalms of Solomon 14:2): in the Psalms of Solomon the righteous themselves are God's garden, rooted forever.

In the Psalms of Solomon Hades is no longer the common home of the dead but the sinners' lot: "their inheritance is Hades, darkness and destruction" (Psalms of Solomon 14:6; compare 15:11), while the devout "inherit life".
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 14:6; Psalms of Solomon 15:11; Psalms of Solomon 16:2

sections.h: The foreign man and the captives sent west (Psalms of Solomon 17)
sections.b: Psalms of Solomon 17 tells how God raised up "a man foreign to our race" against the kings who took David's throne (Psalms of Solomon 17:9), how "the lawless one" emptied the land and sent its people "as far as the west" (Psalms of Solomon 17:13-14). Gray identified him with Pompey, who carried Aristobulus II and his children captive to Rome, and cites Josephus for the captives. For the siege itself see Psalms 2 and 8.
Psalms of Solomon 12 prays against "the law-breaking, whispering tongue that speaks lies and tricks", whose words spread like fire and set households against each other (Psalms of Solomon 12:1-4).
"Blow the trumpet in Zion" (Psalms of Solomon 11:1) takes the opening of the Greek Joel 2:1 and turns the alarm into the signal for the scattered to come home, as in Isaiah 27:13.
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 11:1-2; Joel 2:1; Isaiah 27:13; Matthew 24:31

sections.h: Headings in the Psalms of Solomon 9-18
sections.b: The headings of Psalms of Solomon 9-18 name Solomon and the kind of song ("a psalm", "a hymn", "with a song") and sometimes a purpose: "for correction" (9:0), "for waiting in hope" (11:0), "comfort for the righteous" (13:0), "for help for the devout" (16:0), "for the king" (17:0), "again, of the Lord's Messiah" (18:0). Ryle and James thought whoever wrote the titles may also have added the two Selahs (17:31; 18:10).
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 9:0; Psalms of Solomon 11:0; Psalms of Solomon 17:0; Psalms of Solomon 18:0

sections.h: The lights that keep their path
sections.b: Psalms of Solomon 18:11-14 praises God who set the lights "to mark the times of the hours"; they have never left their path "except when God commanded them by the order of his servants", a likely allusion to Joshua 10 and Isaiah 38.
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 18:11-14; Genesis 1:14; Psalm 148:6; Joshua 10:13
